analysis.one_liner: Creates a national paid family and medical leave insurance program run through Social Security.
analysis.headline: The bill has 207 of 217 House Democrats as cosponsors, but the Republican-run Ways and Means Committee has not acted on it, so no vote has ever been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The FAMILY Act would create a federal paid leave insurance program, administered by the Social Security Administration, that pays workers a share of their wages — up to $4,000 a month — while they take time off for a new child, their own serious illness, or to care for a family member with a serious health condition. It would also protect people who take leave from being fired and require their jobs and health coverage to be there when they return. The program would be funded through the same Social Security payroll taxes workers and employers already pay, with a new contribution added. The bill was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has not taken it up.
analysis.who_benefits: Working people who need time off — new parents, workers facing their own serious illness, and people caring for sick spouses, children, parents, or other family members — would get monthly wage-replacement checks (85% of earnings at the lower tiers, capped at $4,000 a month) while keeping job protection and health coverage. Self-employed workers and people who have lost a job also qualify. Workers in low-wage jobs benefit most, since they are the least likely to have any paid leave from an employer today.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers without paid leave, especially low-wage workers

how_it_helps.text: Provides up to about 12 months of monthly cash benefits for a qualifying caregiving period, with monthly benefits of roughly 85% of earnings for lower earners, capped at $4,000 a month and floored at $580 a month.

Covers care for a newborn or newly adopted or foster child, care for a wide circle of family members with a serious health condition, the worker's own serious health condition, and leave related to domestic violence, sexual assault, stalking, and trafficking.

Makes it unlawful for an employer to fire, discipline, or retaliate against a worker for using the benefit, requires restoration to the same or an equivalent job, and requires employers to keep health coverage in force during leave.
Covers self-employed people and workers who have lost their jobs, not just employees of large firms, and lets workers claim benefits retroactively for care in the prior 90 days.
Does not displace stronger state programs or better employer or union benefits; states with existing paid-leave programs get federal grants to keep them running.

analysis.who_pays: The program is financed through the Social Security payroll taxes referenced in the bill text — meaning workers and employers would each pay a share of a new payroll contribution. Employers would also carry the cost of holding jobs open and complying with the law's anti-retaliation and job-restoration rules.
analysis.who_pays_short: Workers and employers, through payroll taxes

drawbacks.text: The program is funded through the Social Security payroll taxes paid by employees and employers, which means a permanent tax increase on wages; economists generally note payroll taxes fall heavily on workers themselves through lower take-home pay.

Employers bear new compliance obligations — job restoration, continued health coverage, and anti-retaliation rules — and face damages including 60 days of wages plus liquidated damages and attorney's fees for violations, a cost small businesses in particular would feel.

Benefits can only be claimed through a documented application and certification process administered by a new federal office, and the bill directs a report on whether application review and payment timelines (as short as 20 days) are even feasible — an acknowledgment that processing speed is a real risk.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is large and real: guaranteed paid leave for births, serious illness, and family care is something the U.S. uniquely lacks among wealthy countries, and the proposed benefit ($580–$4,000/month) replaces a meaningful share of pay for low and middle earners. The costs are real too: a permanent increase in Social Security payroll taxes paid by workers and employers, a new federal bureaucracy, and a compliance and potential-litigation burden on employers, including small ones. The bill is fairly well designed — it protects against retaliation, sets an honest income-replacement formula, and lets existing state programs stand. The honest objection is not design but cost and scope: a permanent new entitlement financed by payroll taxes, in a Congress where it has no Republican support and has never reached a vote in any Congress.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on September 16, 2025 and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, where it has sat with no markup, no vote, and no movement since.

narrative.text: H.R. 5390 was introduced in the House on September 16, 2025 and referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means the same day.
The full action history shows only introduction and referral — no committee markup, no floor vote, and no Senate action.
207 of the House's 217 Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did.
Republicans hold a majority of the Ways and Means Committee and of the House, and the committee has not scheduled the bill for consideration.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, employers who would have owed a new payroll contribution and leave obligations are better off; working people who need paid leave have gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers avoiding a new payroll tax

for.name: Rep. Rosa DeLauro
for.role: Sponsor, House Democratic lead on family policy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FAMILY Act and recruited 207 Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, controlled by Republicans
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in September 2025 and has taken no action on it since — no markup, no hearing, no vote.

against.name: Business lobbies such as the U.S. Chamber of Commerce
against.what_they_did: Have historically opposed national paid-leave mandates on cost grounds; no bill-specific campaign appears in the record.

against.name: House Republicans
against.what_they_did: No House Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Support is entirely Democratic — 207 of 217 House Democrats cosponsored — while no Republican sponsored or cosponsored the bill.

industries.note: Employers would pay a share of a new payroll tax and take on new duties to hold jobs open, maintain health coverage during leave, and avoid retaliation liability. These costs fall on businesses of every size.
A new federal benefit administered by a new Social Security office would create compliance and claims-processing work that third-party administrators and consultants help employers handle.

More people could take time off to receive or arrange treatment, and providers must certify serious health conditions, adding paperwork but also supporting patients who currently skip care because they cannot miss work.

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican House majority, a Republican-controlled Ways and Means Committee, and zero Republican cosponsors, the bill is very unlikely to get a committee markup or a floor vote this Congress, and if unreported from committee it will die when the Congress ends in January 2027 — the same fate as earlier versions of the FAMILY Act.
